secondary_sources.title: Timbuktu and the Songhay Empire: A Catalogue of the Sources

contested_points: Surviving chronicles disagree on whether birth fell in the mid-1550s or slightly later.
Colonial-era retellings sometimes blur voluntary study travel with forced exile after the 1591 invasion.
known_myths: He was not the only major scholar in sixteenth-century Timbuktu; Sankore hosted many teachers and students.
Popular lists on the internet misattribute modern political quotes to his Arabic corpus.

retrieval_cards.text: Arabic sources describe Ahmed Baba as a jurist and teacher associated with Sankore and wider Timbuktu scholarly networks before the Moroccan invasion of Songhai.
His bibliographical work Nayl al-ibtihaj catalogues West African authors and works; it is used by historians to trace intellectual networks across the Sahel.
After the 1591 Moroccan campaign against Songhai, Ahmed Baba was among scholars taken to Marrakesh; surviving accounts describe captivity, teaching, and petitions for return.

Scholarship records his teaching of Maliki jurisprudence and related disciplines to students in Timbuktu and later in Morocco; language-learning quests may introduce Arabic phrases only from approved teaching notes.
He died in Marrakesh in 1627 according to standard chronicles cited in modern catalogues; exact calendar conversion varies by edition.
His life spans the late Songhai empire and Moroccan control of Timbuktu; learners should separate imperial politics from everyday scholarly life in the city.
